title: Karna's abandonment
hook: a charioteer and his wife find a basket on the river, and raise the boy inside as their own
carry: let go upstream, taken in downstream

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shining baby in a basket, and a frightened mother blessing him from the bank. A person on each side of it.

Downstream, a man and his wife are by the water. He's Adhiratha, a charioteer, a suta, whose work is driving and caring for the chariots of warriors. She's Radha. The text tells us they have no child. Floating toward them comes a basket. They pull it to the bank, open it, and find a baby boy, glowing, in armor and earrings. Yesterday we stood with the mother who let go. Today we stand with the parents who catch.
screen: `DOWNSTREAM: ADHIRATHA AND RADHA.` → `A BASKET ON THE WATER.` → `A BOY INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Adhiratha and Radha take the boy home and raise him as their son. There's no long debate in the telling. They wanted a child, and here is one. They name him Vasusena, a name that points back to the armor and earrings he was born with. Later the world will know him as Karna. He's also called Radheya, son of Radha, after the woman who raised him, not the one who bore him. Hold onto that name. Here's what the river has done. Karna was born to a princess and a god, and has grown up in a charioteer's house. In the world of the Mahabharata, that matters. Birth decides a great deal: who may compete, who may rule, who gets laughed at. For most of his life Karna will carry royal blood he doesn't know about, and a charioteer's home he will not disown. Both will be pressed on him by others, and both are part of who he is. Abandonment is only half of this story. The other half is adoption. A child let go upstream is taken in downstream, and Karna will carry both halves all his life: the loss from upstream, and the home from downstream.
screen: `TAKEN IN AS THEIR OWN.` · `VASUSENA, AND KARNA.` · `RADHEYA: SON OF RADHA.` · `A PRINCE'S BLOOD, A CHARIOTEER'S HOME.` · then, large: `LET GO UPSTREAM, TAKEN IN DOWNSTREAM.`

segments.voice: Someone once took you in when they didn't have to: a teacher, a neighbor, a friend's family, a stepparent. Picture their face, and remember one specific kindness, the smallest you can find. Let it sit in the chest, without needing words.
Karna's abandonment. A basket caught downstream, a charioteer and his wife, and a boy named Vasusena, Radheya, Karna.
Your line: let go upstream, taken in downstream. Two mothers, one river. Day seven hundred thirty, done.

howItsDone: In retellings, Karna is also called Radheya, son of Radha, honoring the mother who raised him; listeners meet him under that name as well as Karna.

what it means: a child let go upstream and taken in downstream by a charioteer and his wife.
what a scholar hears: the name Radheya keeps the adoptive mother in his name, and his charioteer upbringing will shape how others treat him.

chat.says: Why is Karna also called Radheya?
options: It means son of Radha, the charioteer's wife who raised him as her own.
It means son of the river, because he was found floating in a basket.
It means son of the sun, because Surya was his father all along.
chat.meaning: Adhiratha and his wife Radha found the basket and raised the boy. Radheya means son of Radha, the woman who raised him.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that the text says Adhiratha and Radha were childless when they found him.
The name Vasusena is linked to the armor and earrings he was born with; no etymology of 'vasu' is stated. Confirm the text gives this link.
Radheya glossed as 'son of Radha'; confirm.
The claim that birth decides who may compete and rule is the script's framing of later scenes (the tournament); confirm it is fair.
howItsDone: 'often called Radheya' is a general claim about retellings; a Keeper may soften further.
